stops.name: New Delhi, the letters to Miguel Serrano
stops.campa: Across the world, in Chile, Miguel Serrano is building his own Esoteric Hitlerism, and the two elders of the same strange faith exchange letters in her last years. She writes to him on the twenty-eighth of March of their loneliness, we are so few in this immense, indifferent world, and of her doctrine of the avatar: that the man she worshipped had too much Sun and not enough Lightning, and that only the last one, Kalki, will hold both in perfect balance and win. Though they never fully read each other, they recognise one another as kin, two keepers of the golden thread.
stops.quote: He had in Him 'too much Sun, not enough Lightning,' because only the last one (the one the Hindu Scriptures call the 'Kalki' avatar) will be equally Sun and Lightning, and will win.

stops.name: New Delhi, the last letter, calling for death the liberator
stops.campa: On the twentieth of April, again the birthday of her god, she writes to Serrano for the last time, half-blind and longing to be gone. Her right eye is already gone, she tells him, and the left is going the same way; every day, she writes, she calls for death, the liberator. She is worn to nothing by age and poverty, yet unrepentant, her creed intact. Within half a year the liberator will come. The final letter closes a correspondence that binds her mythology to Serrano's, the two great voices of Esoteric Hitlerism speaking across the ocean as the light in her fails.
stops.quote: I see almost nothing. My right eye is already kaputt, and now the left is going the same way... Every day I call for death, the liberator!

stops.name: Sible Hedingham, death in an English village
stops.campa: Bound at last for America to speak to her comrades, she breaks her journey in the Essex village of Sible Hedingham, at the house of a friend, and there, shortly after midnight on the twenty-second of October, her heart stops. She is seventy-seven, near-blind, and poor, dying far from Greece and from India in a quiet English lane. Her comrades will say the priestess of the Sun went out with the year's light failing, faithful to the end to the god she served and the avatar she never lived to see.

stops.name: Colchester, the pyre
stops.campa: At Colchester her body is given to the fire, as she wished, in the manner of the faith she took in India: no cross, no priest of the Galilean, only the flame that to her is the Sun's own agent, dissolving the flesh and freeing whatever burns on. The chemist who worshipped Life as energy, the pagan who kept the solstices, returns to the elements she adored. Her ashes are gathered into an inscribed urn and made ready for a long last voyage across the Atlantic.

stops.name: Arlington, the ashes carried to the altar
stops.campa: On the twentieth of February her urn is carried to Arlington in Virginia, to the headquarters of the American movement, and set upon an altar beside the remains of Rockwell in what her followers call a hall of honour. So the priestess who was born by the Rhône, made pagan at Delphi, reborn as a Hindu goddess on the Indian shore, and imprisoned in the ruins of the Reich, comes to rest at last as a relic upon a shrine. In the register of her own creed the wheel has not stopped: she waits there, they say, for the avatar of the end and the return of the gold.
